description:
## Outcome

The daemon owns a random per-user authentication token and an atomic discovery record with its loopback port, PID, runtime version, and protocol version.

## Why now

Clients need secure discovery before the loopback server can accept requests. Stale records and weak permissions can connect a client to the wrong process or expose the token.

## Work

1. Generate the token from a cryptographic random source and store it under the resolved state root.
2. Restrict token and discovery access to the current user with Unix permissions or the Windows access-control capability.
3. Write discovery state atomically only after the server owns its port.
4. Validate record schema, PID identity, protocol version, and daemon liveness before use.
5. Remove stale state with a race-safe lock or compare-and-delete rule.
6. Remove owned discovery state on clean stop without deleting a newer daemon record.
7. Redact the token and private paths from all errors, logs, and portable results.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The token has sufficient entropy and is never accepted from argv.
- [ ] Another local user cannot read the token through supported platform controls.
- [ ] Concurrent daemon starts produce one owner and one clear failure.
- [ ] A stale or corrupt record is repaired safely.
- [ ] Clean stop removes only the record owned by that daemon instance.
- [ ] Tests cover spaces, non-ASCII profiles, short writes, rename failures, and permission failures.

## Tests

Use injected random, clock, PID, file-system, permission, and liveness capabilities. Run `mix quality`, `mix test --cover`, and `mix docs`.

## Non-goals

Do not bind a public interface. Do not place secrets in `release.json` or JSONL.
title: Store daemon authentication and discovery state securely
